claims.text: High configurational entropy governs structural stability in nanoalloys at high temperatures.
High configurational entropy governs chemical stability in nanoalloys at high temperatures.
Sluggish atomic diffusion at the nanoscale contributes to high-temperature stability.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion minimize phase separation.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion minimize surface segregation.
A near-equal distribution of five or more elements produces a higher-configurational-entropy nanoalloy than a composition deliberately skewed away from equiatomic ratios.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation effects during annealing at 800–1000 °C.
Greater atomic-level mixing suppresses diffusion-driven grain growth.
Greater atomic-level mixing suppresses surface segregation.
High mixing entropy lowers the free energy of a uniformly mixed solid solution.
High mixing entropy retards atomic migration through sluggish diffusion.
Retarded atomic migration reduces the kinetic tendency toward phase separation and surface segregation.
Lowering configurational entropy allows atomic-size and surface-energy differences to promote segregation and phase instability.
After identical annealing, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a more uniform, single-phase microstructure than lower-entropy controls.
After identical annealing, high-entropy nanoalloys will show less chemical segregation than lower-entropy controls.
After identical annealing, high-entropy nanoalloys will show less grain coarsening than lower-entropy controls.
The prediction is bounded to nanoscale particles annealed at 800–1000 °C under inert atmospheres.
Oxidizing conditions may alter the predicted behavior.
Significantly larger particles may behave differently because surface effects are less dominant.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome treats the lower-entropy alloys as the comparison baseline, whereas the explicit baseline field identifies the near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys as the baseline.
